items.description:
### Summary
A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted `publicKey` inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

### Details
`packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts` `readLength()` parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to `buf.byteLength`, and `readInteger()` then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

```ts
function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}
```

  by typing in the Curator media-picker search box. The search query omitted the tenant ownership scope that the

  The issue was introduced in v3.2.4, when multitenancy support was added to the media picker.

AWS-advanced-jdbc-wrapper: Java Deserialization RCE via Cache Poisoning
items.description:
### Impact
The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source JDBC driver wrapper that extends a JDBC driver to enable Amazon Aurora and AWS Cloud features such as failover handling and caching. We identified CVE-2026-14265, an issue in the RemoteQueryCachePlugin of the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper. When this plugin is enabled, query results read from the shared Redis/Valkey cache are deserialized without class filtering. An actor with write access to the shared cache infrastructure could insert a crafted serialized Java object that, when read by an application, results in execution of arbitrary code on the application server.

### Workarounds
The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by disabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, and by restricting write access to the Redis/Valkey cache infrastructure to trusted principals

items.title: pympp allows excessive sponsored transaction fees through padded calldata
items.description:
### Details
When the server acts as the fee_payer, `pympp` 0.8.0 validates calldata using `eth_abi` decoding, which is lenient about trailing bytes. The `FeePayerPolicy` caps `gas_limit` (≤ 2 M) and `max_fee_per_gas` (≤ 100 Gwei) but does **not** check calldata length.

Tempo uses legacy calldata gas pricing: **16 gas per non-zero byte**. Appending `N` bytes of `0x01` padding inflates actual gas used by `N × 16` while keeping `gas_limit` and `max_fee_per_gas` within policy caps. The server cosigns and broadcasts the padded transaction, draining its fee-payer wallet.

**Vulnerable code path:** `FeePayerPolicy` in `fee_payer_policy.py` (pympp 0.8.0) enforces `maxGas = 2_000_000` and `maxFeePerGas = 100 Gwei` but has no `calldata.length` bound. The policy check passes because the inflated gas comes from intrinsic calldata cost, not the declared `gas_limit`.

items.title: Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata
items.description:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer `'use cache'` function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner `'use cache'` call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via `next/root-params`) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

items.description:
## Summary

`qbee-agent` contains a Zip Slip vulnerability in `app/utils/tar.go`. The tar extractor checks whether an entry remains inside the destination directory with:

```go
strings.HasPrefix(targetPath, destdirClean)
```

This does not enforce a path separator boundary. If the destination directory is `/tmp/.../context`, a tar entry such as `../context-outside/payload.txt` cleans to `/tmp/.../context-outside/payload.txt` and still passes the prefix check. qbee-agent then creates the outside directory and writes the payload outside the intended extraction root.

The issue is reachable through the Docker Compose build context path when `UseContext` is enabled.

- `1d8bdbb7422adb4ca563d3114cbe2817d6ba3581`

items.description:
### Summary

A non-admin user who can update their own shares can reassign a share's creator (`user_created`), `role`, `item`, and `collection` fields after the share is created. The update is authorized against the row as it existed before the change, and the resulting row is never revalidated, so these fields can be set to values the user would not be permitted to assign when creating a share. By reassigning both `user_created` and `role` to an administrator the share's effective permissions get elevated.

This is a server-side authorization gap in the share update path. It does not by itself produce an administrator token. It re-opens a previously patched privilege-escalation surface on the effective permissions of a share.

items.title: mail-parser: One hostile attachment aborts `write_attachments()` and silently drops the rest of the batch
items.description:
### Impact

`write_attachments()` called `_safe_attachment_filename()` and `write_sample()` inside its loop
with no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachment
**after** the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller that
catches only `MailParserError`.

That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned part
first and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory that
a downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail client
intact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the same
failure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass in
[GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496](https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496).

Three shapes were reachable, all from atta

does not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issue
as [GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf](https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf),
which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).

All entry points are affected: `parse_from_string()`, `parse_from_bytes()`, `parse_from_file()`,
`parse_from_file_obj()` and the `mail-parser` CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled and
a single line is enough, so any pipeline that parses untrusted mail can be made to lose the

items.description:
### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address
the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching
can tell them apart:

- the first token of the `from` clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a
  candidate;
- an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
- a candidate must sit inside a `(` / `[` group;
- IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
- the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into
  sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the `IPv6:` tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

items.description:
### Summary

Two regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrack
polynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formed
email can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process that
parses untrusted mail.

Both are reachable from an ordinary `parse_from_string()`, `parse_from_bytes()`
or `parse_from_file()` call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is
required by the victim.

alternative `([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)>` overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent
`\s*` — a space matches both. Driven by `finditer`, which retries at every

items.title: mail-parser: Path Traversal vulnerability in attachment extraction
items.description:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

- Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.
- Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.

items.title: termux-sync: Arbitrary file write during restore via attacker-controlled manifest source path
items.description:
termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.

During restore, each archive entry is handled as:

  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent
  extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)

extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:

  with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf:
      for member in tf.getmembers():
          tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)

There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.

items.title: code-review-mcp-server: Command injection via unsanitized folderPath/baseBranch parameters
items.description:
### Impact

`code-review-mcp-server` exposes MCP tools (`getLocalGitDiff`, `codeReview`, `createPR`, `getPRTemplate`) that accept `folderPath` and `baseBranch` string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via `child_process.execSync()`, which runs commands through `/bin/sh`.

A crafted value such as `baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #"` (or a `$(...)` command substitution, or a `folderPath` that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in **arbitrary command execution** on the host running the MCP server.

### Patches

Fixed in **1.5.3**. Every `execSync()` call was replaced with `execFileSync()` using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to `git` / `gh` without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to `code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3` or later.

items.description:
### Summary

LightSaml 5.0.0 (latest release; also confirmed on 4.6.1) validates an inbound `samlp:Response` by collecting its direct-child `saml:Assertion` elements and validating each one's `ds:Signature` via robrichards/xmlseclibs. An attacker who has captured one genuine signed assertion can exploit this to surface attacker-authored, unsigned claims.

items.title: Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()
items.description:
Next.js applications with `'use cache'` can disclose cached data across root params when the same `'use cache'` function is called both directly during rendering and through `unstable_cache()`, and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an `unstable_cache()` call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. `unstable_cache()` then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

items.title: NLTK dot2img runs Graphviz 'dot' without the trusted-exec chokepoint, enabling local code execution via a writable PATH element
items.description:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.dependencygraph.dot2img` invokes the Graphviz `dot` executable without the trusted-execution guarantees that NLTK applies to its other native-tool wrappers. The function resolves `dot` by bare name and then runs the resolved absolute path with a raw `subprocess.run`, omitting the ownership/writability check and the loader-environment scrub that `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted` provides. On a POSIX host, a local, unprivileged actor who can write to any group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's `PATH` can plant a trojan `dot`; when the victim later renders a `DependencyGraph` (for example in a Jupyter notebook, which auto-invokes `_repr_svg_`) or calls `dot2img` directly, the planted binary executes as the victim. items.title: Nuxt exposes the message and data of unhandled errors thrown during server rendering
items.description:
### Summary

When a page, plugin or route middleware throws an error that is not an HTTP error, Nuxt wraps it with `createError` before rendering the error page. The wrapped error was treated as one the app raised deliberately, so in production its `message` and `data` were sent to the client in the error page payload (`__NUXT_DATA__`) and in JSON error responses. For a failed `$fetch`, that is the URL that was requested (including its query string) and the body of the upstream error response.

### Impact

An application is affected if server-rendered code lets an error with sensitive details reach the error page, for example:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
const route = useRoute()
// the upstream error body, and the token in the URL, reach the client if this request fails
await $fetch(`http://users.internal/users/${route.params.id}?token=${useRuntimeConfig().usersToken}`)
</script>
``

items.title: Nuxt payload URL generation has quadratic cost for repeated slashes in the request path
items.description:
### Summary

Nuxt strips trailing slashes from the request path with a regular expression whose cost grows quadratically with the length of a run of consecutive slashes. A single unauthenticated request with a long run of slashes can occupy the server's event loop for a noticeable time, delaying every other request handled by the same process.

### Impact

When a page is rendered with payload extraction (any route covered by an `isr`, `swr` or `cache` route rule), Nuxt builds the `_payload.json` URL from the raw request path. A path such as `/blog/a` followed by 16,000 slashes and `x`, which fits within Node's default header size limit, takes roughly 0.1 to 0.4 seconds of synchronous CPU time per request, depending on hardware. Concurrent requests to the same process wait for it to finish, so a modest request rate can keep a process saturated.

items.description:
### Summary

`Application.add_domain()` compiled each `*` in a host mask to `[^:]*`. With two or more wildcards in a mask, matching a long `Host` header that does not match the mask took polynomial time on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could stall a server that registers a domain mask with more than one wildcard by sending requests with a long `Host` header.

### Workaround

Use at most one `*` in a domain mask.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43

items.title: AIOHTTP: Unbounded cookie storage in client CookieJar
items.description:
### Summary

`Set-Cookie` parsing created additional cookies from unrecognised `name=value` attributes, and `CookieJar` had no limit on the number of cookies stored or sent. A server could make the client store a very large number of cookies and generate very large `Cookie` headers.

### Impact

A malicious server could cause excessive memory and CPU use in a client, repeated on every redirect, and cause later requests to the same domain to build an excessively large `Cookie` header.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6963ee0befec1502b6bb7b4db6c72d044c08f4fa

items.title: AIOHTTP: Too many URL-encoded form fields block the event loop
items.description:
### Summary

`Request.post()` had no limit on the number of fields in a URL-encoded form body. Inserting a large number of repeated keys into a `MultiDict` took quadratic time on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could block the event loop with a form POST within the default `client_max_size` to any handler that calls `Request.post()`.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/615fec3d4f088f30d2ee72cad760152e92aa1c53

items.title: AIOHTTP: Base64 multipart parts bypass client_max_size
items.description:
### Summary

When reading a multipart part with `Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64`, `BodyPartReader.read_chunk()` kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short `Content-Length`, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could bypass `client_max_size` to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fdd

items.title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket max_msg_size bypass via integer overflow
items.description:
### Summary

The `max_msg_size` check in the WebSocket reader added the declared frame length to the size of the partial message already buffered. In the C extension this addition is 64-bit arithmetic, so a declared length close to 2**63 overflowed and the check passed.

### Impact

An attacker could bypass `max_msg_size` and cause unbounded memory use by streaming an oversized WebSocket message after a small non-final fragment.

### Workaround

If unable to upgrade, the Python reader is unaffected and can be used with `AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1`.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8cfbe9abe5e11b84006a10f9bdf82bf607671dab

items.title: AIOHTTP: Unbounded buffering of data received during an upgrade request
items.description:
### Summary

While a request flagged as an upgrade (e.g. a WebSocket handshake) was being handled, all further data received on the connection was buffered with no size limit or flow control until the handler completed.

### Impact

An attacker could cause unbounded memory use by streaming data behind an upgrade request to any handler that does not immediately accept or reject the upgrade.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/3d850ee9b92573c7e913821cbcb96005beb3f4df

items.title: AIOHTTP: Pure-Python parser request replay and buffer growth behind a declined upgrade
items.description:
### Summary

When the pipelined request queue was full, the pure-Python parser stored the unparsed remainder internally and also returned it to the caller. After a handler declined an upgrade request, the buffered data was re-fed, so the buffer grew with each handled request and already-handled requests were dispatched to the application again.

### Impact

If users are using the Python parser (`AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS`, or not a standard wheel installed), an attacker could cause excessive memory use and cause pipelined requests to be processed more than once.

### Workaround

Switch to the default C parser.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/47babd8c23ca79e2bae6cc8dcb5752b61e369fc7

items.title: AIOHTTP: Concatenated compressed streams cause excessive CPU use
items.description:
### Summary

When decompressing a payload made up of many concatenated compressed members (gzip, deflate or zstd), each member was decoded by passing the entire remaining input to a new decompressor, resulting in quadratic CPU time. Empty members produce no output, so `client_max_size` and output backpressure did not limit the work.

### Impact

An attacker could block the event loop of a server with a specially crafted compressed request body or WebSocket message. A malicious server could do the same to a client.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/d925a80539ffd227da1d93ab4a5bff123cc777db

items.title: AIOHTTP: WebSocket receive queue limits bypassed by small or compressed messages
items.description:
### Summary

The WebSocket reader continued parsing frames already received after the receive queue had paused the transport, and empty messages were not counted towards the queue size. With permessage-deflate, a single read of compressed frames could add many megabytes of decompressed messages to the queue.

### Impact

An attacker could cause excessive memory use in a WebSocket server, or a malicious server against a client, by sending many small or compressed messages faster than the application consumes them.

---

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/0ae507423f681161efa77d20052b4054397c7fb6

items.title: SvelteKit: Private `query.batch` functions could collide, producing unexpected parameter / function combinations
items.description: Under certain circumstances, private (non-exported) `query.batch` functions could end up sharing a batch, resulting in the arguments from one function being passed to another. This only affects apps using the experimental remote functions flag and non-exported `query.batch` functions.

items.title: SvelteKit: Protocol-relative module import during server-side route resolution allows cross-origin script execution
items.description: If an attacker could, using some form of social engineering or other exploit, get a user to use client-side navigation to navigate to a specially-crafted link, the attacker could cause code from another domain to be imported and run on the user's machine. This only affected apps with `router.resolution: 'server'`.

items.title: NLTK: Symlink escape in chat80.sql_query bypasses the pathsec data-root sandbox to read out-of-root SQLite databases
items.description:
## Summary

`nltk.sem.chat80.sql_query()` opens a SQLite database by handing the result of `nltk.data.find(dbname)` straight to `sqlite3.connect()` without the path-containment check that the NLTK data sandbox (`nltk.pathsec`) is meant to enforce. `nltk.data.find()` applies only lexical checks to the resource name and returns a `FileSystemPathPointer` whose path is normalized with `os.path.abspath` but never resolved for symlinks. As a result, an in-root symbolic link that points at a SQLite file outside every registered NLTK data root is followed by SQLite, and the caller receives query results from the out-of-sandbox database. An attacker who can place a file inside a directory the application trusts as an NLTK data root can read SQLite databases that the pathsec sandbox is supposed to keep out of reach.

## Root Cause

The security invariant is that file access performed through NLTK

items.title: NLTK: Path Traversal in save_maxent_params / load_maxent_params Allow Arbitrary File READ/WRITE
items.description:
### Summary
Path traversal in NLTK's save_maxent_params() and load_maxent_params() allows arbitrary file write and arbitrary file read outside the directories permitted by NLTK's pathsec security mechanism.

This vulnerability was previously reported through Huntr, accepted by the NLTK project, and assigned CVE-2026-15367. A $750 bounty was paid through Huntr (i didnt get the fix bounty). Huntr subsequently shut down its OSS vulnerability program, so I am submitting this report through GitHub to continue the existing disclosure process and preserve the original CVE assignment and researcher credit.

### Details
The affected functions are:

- nltk.classify.maxent.load_maxent_params()
- nltk.classify.maxent.save_maxent_params()
